speakers.name: David Chiaverini
speakers.title: Analyst
speakers.firm: Jefferies (introduced by the operator as RBC Capital Markets; corrected himself)

exchanges.question: On the AI cash tool discussed in the Chairman's letter, which could pressure consumer deposits, increase competition and raise deposit betas, how does Jamie see deposit competition unfolding as similar smart tools spread? Follow-up on the Basel III proposal: does the capital guidance contemplate mitigating actions on RWA inflation, and what magnitude of SCB relief could come from removing the double counting of market and operational risk?
exchanges.answer: Jamie: it is early stages and must be viewed segment by segment; higher-net-worth clients are astute and have many choices, and the aim is to make managing money easier within a whole basket of value (ATMs, branches, advice, Zelle); it may squeeze some margin and create competition somewhere, but that is life, and there is tons of competition for money. Jeremy: deposit competition has always been intense from external and internal higher-yielding alternatives; the tool is not even live yet, targets a very small subset of clients with investments where the firm hopes to win a larger share of the investment wallet, and should be viewed as an experiment. On Basel, the firm is well-practiced at deploying resources efficiently and hopes the final rules do not make healthy businesses non-economic; targeted RWA clarifications are needed on high-yield repo collateral and advised lines, this is not an optimization story, and G-SIB is the one area that significantly disincentivises certain markets businesses and the depth of U.S. capital markets. On the double count, the firm is currently below the floor, so relief via stress testing would have no impact while changes to operational risk RWA might; it is unclear whether JPMorgan will be structurally below the floor, and removal is supported but not the top priority. Jamie added the Global Market Shock has never resembled the real world, the firm already holds $80 billion or $90 billion of capital for trading books, and operational risk capital is a crazy, obtuse one-in-1,000-year construct that creates artificial RWA that persists even after exiting a business.

exchanges.question: Having cut the markets NII outlook for the change in rates, why was the $95 billion NII ex-Markets outlook retained given asset sensitivity, and what offsets higher rates if there are no cuts the rest of the year? Follow-up to Jamie: if a recession brings higher defaults and losses in leveraged lending, what is the ultimate loss to banks, and would a private credit default cycle be systemic?
exchanges.answer: Jeremy: the just-disclosed EAR is $1.8 billion, but because the removed cuts were back-dated the impact on the full-year average rate is only about 20 basis points, so the implied upward revision was quite small and was absorbed by other noise and rounding; nothing to read into. Jamie: no, not systemic; private credit leveraged lending is about $1.7 trillion, high yield bonds about $1.7 trillion, bank syndicated leveraged loans about $1.7 trillion, versus investment grade debt of $13 trillion and mortgage debt of about $13 trillion. There has been some weakening in underwriting beyond private credit, a credit cycle will come one day with losses worse than people expect relative to the scenario, but at that size it almost cannot be systemic and banks would need very large private credit losses before being hit; the bigger worry is how a cycle filters through the whole system, while corporate and consumer debt is not too high and the excess debt sits with governments. Every cycle surprises in some industry (utilities and telecom in 2000, media and newspapers in 2008), and this time it might or might not be software.

exchanges.question: How did scenario weighting and evolving macro risk views factor into reserve setting this quarter? Follow-up: given very strong balance sheet growth, largely in Markets, what drove it and what is the outlook for loan and deposit growth this year?
exchanges.answer: Scenario weights were not changed this quarter; unchanged weights flowing through the economic outlook lowered the weighted average unemployment rate in the allowance from 5.8% to 5.6%, creating tailwinds mainly in consumer and a little in wholesale, plus a home lending release of about $150 million (maybe $110 million) from an HPI upward revision, partly offset by wholesale builds from loan growth and idiosyncratic downgrades. The firm consciously debated adding downside skew given the Middle East and concluded the existing conservative bias was sufficient; downside outcomes such as higher energy prices would flow naturally through the process. Balance sheet growth was primarily Markets, low-density secured financing that adds little RWA and is largely seasonal, on top of a background trend of Markets growth. The most significant loan outlook number is card loan growth of 6% or maybe a little more, unchanged from Company Update; growth elsewhere is modest with Home Lending headwinds from First Republic portfolio roll-off and some acquisition financing held on balance sheet; Markets has been the primary driver of wholesale loan growth, mainly opportunistic data center lending where the firm will walk away if terms do not make sense. Deposit growth was not addressed in this answer.

exchanges.question: How resilient are consumer spend and credit if energy prices stay high, and are there any signs of cracks? Follow-up: any signs of bad volatility in trading in March, and was the large quarter-on-quarter rise in trading assets driven by the environment or by the ongoing deployment of excess capital?
exchanges.answer: Jeremy: nothing new to say; early roll rates, delinquencies, cash buffers, and discretionary and non-discretionary spend are all consistent with prior trends and fundamentally healthy. Gas or energy is roughly 3% of the typical consumer's expenditure in the portfolio, and no visible trade-down in other discretionary spend has appeared yet; the biggest reason for healthy consumer credit is the strong labor market, and bad Middle East outcomes or much higher energy prices would show up only if they eventually hit the labor market. Jamie added the consumer is also being helped by higher tax refunds. On trading, there has been no broad bad volatility (gappy, illiquid markets that sideline clients), which helped performance; the trading asset growth was mostly business-as-usual, seasonal, low-risk-density, and not a function of capital deployment, which would be a longer-term phenomenon requiring both capital and liquidity to be freed up.

exchanges.question: Of the $1.7 trillion private credit market, how much is substitution from banks versus credit banks would never have originated, can banks recapture share, what is JPMorgan doing on collateral given headlines of more conservatism, and are spreads improving? Follow-up to Jeremy: with consumer deposits up 2% after an air pocket, is this the start of a return to higher deposit growth?
exchanges.answer: Jamie: the trillion was always there and banks did it before being discouraged from leveraged lending above certain leverage; probably half was arbitrage that banks could pick up, and banks view the whole relationship (payments, custody, asset management), so some may come back but he is not concerned. Spreads vary by bank and have moved up and down, with loans migrating back and forth between private credit and the syndicated market; the firm has always had marking rights on underlying collateral, actual credit has not gotten much worse except in pockets, and he does not think it is systemic, but when the broader credit cycle comes (driven by underwriting, leverage, PIKs and competition) performance will not be a bell curve, some players will prove weak and business will come back to banks. Jeremy: air pocket is a strong word, but it is too early to declare robust consumer deposit growth is back given tax season support; the expectation of low to mid-single-digit consumer deposit growth is unchanged, over 450,000 net new checking accounts were added this quarter, and yield-seeking flows remain the swing factor. On wholesale, last year was exceptionally strong, expectations for this year were more modest, but the year is starting well as year-end seasonal balances have not rolled off as much as expected; the core view remains significantly less robust growth than last year.

exchanges.question: First-quarter expenses were elevated relative to the annualized $105 billion full-year guide; how will the next three quarters be brought down to hit it? Follow-up: where do digital assets and stablecoins go in terms of deposit impact and, more importantly, payments?
exchanges.answer: Jeremy discouraged annualizing quarterly expenses because of seasonality in volume and revenue-related expense, and said the firm does not hunt for cuts to hit guidance but manages expenses holistically. Given the exceptionally strong Markets and Banking performance, one might have expected an upward revision; investors should not assume the implied internal offset between revenue-related and other expenses will hold for the full year, it is early, and if every quarter were as good the firm would spend more than $105 billion for good reason; the $105 billion is not a promise but an outcome of business results. On stablecoins, the wholesale business is already innovating through Kinexys with programmable money, extended hours and tokenized deposits; stablecoins will not radically disrupt wholesale payments, which is already a very efficient, technologically sophisticated, low-margin business. On the consumer side the use case is digital cash with KYC implications, and the key legislative issue is whether rewards act as a proxy for interest, which would turn stablecoins into regulatory arbitrage to run a bank without prudential and consumer protections; the firm supports legislative certainty, wants the same product and risk regulated the same way, and no giant arbitrage backdoor around the prohibition on paying interest.

exchanges.question: Interest-bearing consumer deposit costs fell nicely in the quarter; what is the opportunity going forward given changes in the forward curve? Follow-up: remind us of the structure of private credit loans, including typical advance rates and embedded credit enhancement protecting the bank's position.
exchanges.answer: Jeremy suspected the cost decline simply reflects the rate curve flowing through from last year. Jamie: keep it simple, the deposit margin should be about what it is today, give or take a couple of basis points, with factors like account mix and tax refunds. Jeremy: the yield curve flows through the high-beta portions of the deposit franchise, while the low-beta portion is already priced quite low with little room to price down, as part of a service bundle delivering value to lower-balance clients. On private credit structures, Jamie said that was asking for too much information: they are senior loans on top of leveraged loans, each differs in loan-to-value and triggers, and BDC disclosures provide detail; Jeremy added the positions are senior and diversified with conservative advance rates, good underwriting, sector concentration caps and cash flow trapping, so the firm is quite comfortable although nothing is riskless; Jamie noted BDCs face statutory leverage limits at the parent of roughly one times, sometimes a little more.

exchanges.question: On AI risk: given headlines about LLM-enabled cyber risk being discussed in D.C., is this a different level of risk, how prepared is the banking system, and what would an incident mean systemically? Follow-up on the opportunity side: how meaningful could the AI productivity boost be for the long-term efficiency ratio, and does AI extend JPMorgan's business perimeter into new areas?
exchanges.answer: Jamie: cyber is the firm's largest risk, as stated in the Chairman's letter; JPMorgan is very well protected, spends heavily, has top experts and is in constant contact with government, but AI has made it worse and harder; the firm is testing Mythos, which creates additional vulnerabilities and perhaps future defensive tools. The risk spans every industry and the exchanges and infrastructure banks rely on; banks in total are rather well protected, though not everything they depend on is, and much of it is hygiene (testing software, protecting data, networks and passcodes). Jeremy: generative AI's dual cyber role has been understood for some time; the latest Anthropic models have heightened attention but this is a continuum. On efficiency, Jamie said it is a bad idea to expect AI to improve the efficiency ratio because in a competitive world everyone deploys it and the benefits pass to the marketplace; a head start is possible but not a permanent 50% ROE. On opportunities, absolutely: Connected Commerce (travel, offers) using client data, reducing risk, fraud and scams, better prospecting, AI services to clients, and more adjacencies if used quickly and wisely.

exchanges.question: Why has trading been so consistently strong across good and bad markets and shocks in commodities, rates, credit and equities, with clients also managing well? Follow-up: with a big buffer over required capital, strong capital generation and solid buybacks, any updated thoughts on capital allocation going forward?
exchanges.answer: Jamie: the firm buys and sells almost $4 trillion a day, earning a little each time and managing the exposures; being on the wrong side occasionally is the cost of doing business, like a retailer's unsold inventory, and higher volume and volatility generally widen spreads; the business serves investors with $350 trillion, and the firm never panics over losing trades taken to serve clients. Jeremy: the firm is deploying a ton more capital in Markets, returns are good though below the company's 17%, and it is not getting giant revenue growth on a static capital base. On capital, Jamie said excess capital is measured at around $40 billion today, subject to final rules; the preference is deploying it to serve clients through more bankers, the innovation economy, global and overseas commercial banking, new countries, payment systems and branches, building businesses over time rather than deploying capital as a goal. The world's capital needs (remilitarization, infrastructure, large mergers, companies the firm is not big enough to serve) will create opportunity over time with no rush; buying back stock is not the preferred use today, he would rather buy at a real discount, and he wants to remove the cash returned to investors line from the presentation because it implies buybacks are always good.

exchanges.question: Do the large long-duration capital needs Jamie described favor private markets balance sheets or can big public banks finance them, how do higher-for-longer rates affect the refinancing of BB and B direct lending credits, and can JPMorgan size its private credit exposure?
exchanges.answer: Jeremy sized exposure first: last quarter's walk took NBFI exposure from $330 in the call report to $160 of core NBFI; within that about $50 is private credit, essentially lending to leveraged loan investors (back leverage, BDC lending) with underwriting, diversification and cash flow trapping; a broader leveraged loan back-leverage definition is about $60 billion, with direct lending and subscription lines variously in or out of other measures. Jamie: banks will not warehouse very long-dated assets; private and public markets will converge for investment grade and large non-investment grade, private credit will find large IG harder though it has done it, and the firm presents direct lending side by side with syndicated loans; pension plans and similar institutions need long-dated assets and the firm's job is to intermediate, with on-balance-sheet holdings shorter dated, amid dramatically rising infrastructure needs (utilities, roads, bridges, data centers, GPUs). On higher-for-longer, basic risk management requires preparing for recession and stagflation; higher rates for longer with gapping credit spreads would stress leveraged companies on refinancing, fixed through more capital or lower CapEx rather than overnight disaster; he expects a credit cycle to be worse than people think relative to the scenario, but not systemic and traditional recessionary behavior.

exchanges.question: Did investment banking activity hold up in March, has anything paused or been pushed out of the pipeline, and what is the near-to-intermediate outlook? Follow-up: with the Markets balance sheet up over 20% year-over-year, does the G-SIB surcharge impinge on JPMorgan's ability to grow it, and how does it factor into capital decisions in Markets?
exchanges.answer: Activity held up well; some of the robust quarter reflected accelerated M&A deal closings on faster-than-expected regulatory approval, unrelated to sentiment. The pipeline is resilient, maybe surprisingly so, with Middle East timelines short enough that clients are proceeding in hope of quick resolution; if things derail he would expect an impact on sentiment and deal decisions. On G-SIB, the short answer is yes, it impinges, which is why so much time was spent on the surcharge: it disproportionately hits Markets and the low-risk-density activity clients need, regulators should think carefully about their objectives, and the firm will use its brainpower to serve clients while reducing the G-SIB charge, which is usually called arbitrage and whose outcome is not great for the system. Jamie concurred.

exchanges.question: Agreeing private credit is not systemic, how does JPMorgan ensure it selects top-tier projects and stays with good counterparties while avoiding bad ones?
exchanges.answer: The firm is quite disciplined on credit and turns down deals where it dislikes the covenants, underwriting or the ability to move assets out of the secured company; it is perfectly willing to let its balance sheet shrink and will not make loans if credit is getting stretched, because it will not meet those terms. For most clients including private credit it underwrites the company, the loans and the covenants; credit is a discipline and loans are an outcome of doing good business, and the firm would be completely fine if the loan book dropped 10% next year because it walked away from irresponsible loans.
